claim: Young L-MSCs support the efficient formation of alveolospheres when co-cultured with young or aged AEC2s.
source: In contrast to L-MSCs from aged mice, young L-MSCs support the efficient formation of alveolospheres when co-cultured with young or aged AEC2s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alveolosphere assay shown in Figure 1H-J, demonstrating that young L-MSCs enable alveolosphere formation regardless of AEC2 age.

claim: Aged L-MSCs demonstrated features of cellular senescence.
source: Aged L-MSCs demonstrated features of cellular senescence, altered bioenergetics, and a senescence-associated secretory profile (SASP).
evidence: This claim is supported by β-galactosidase staining (Figure 2A) and lipofuscin staining (Figure 2B) showing senescence markers in aged L-MSCs.

claim: Aged L-MSCs demonstrated altered bioenergetics.
source: Aged L-MSCs demonstrated features of cellular senescence, altered bioenergetics, and a senescence-associated secretory profile (SASP).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data showing altered OCR and ECAR in aged L-MSCs (Figure 3A-H) and reduced ATP/ADP ratios (Figure 3J).

claim: Aged L-MSCs demonstrated a senescence-associated secretory profile (SASP).
source: Aged L-MSCs demonstrated features of cellular senescence, altered bioenergetics, and a senescence-associated secretory profile (SASP).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine array data (Figure 2C-E) and mass spectrometry proteomics (Figure 2F-I) showing elevated SASP factors in aged L-MSCs.

claim: NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4) was highly activated in aged L-MSCs.
source: The reactive oxygen species generating enzyme, NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4), was highly activated in aged L-MSCs and Nox4 downregulation was sufficient to, at least partially, reverse this age-related energy deficit, while restoring the self-organizing capacity of alveolospheres.
evidence: This claim is supported by H2O2 release assay data (Figure 4A) showing higher H2O2 release from aged L-MSCs, which is Nox4-dependent as shown by reduction in Nox4-/+ cells (Figure 4B-C).

claim: Nox4 downregulation was sufficient to, at least partially, reverse the age-related energy deficit in L-MSCs.
source: The reactive oxygen species generating enzyme, NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4), was highly activated in aged L-MSCs and Nox4 downregulation was sufficient to, at least partially, reverse this age-related energy deficit, while restoring the self-organizing capacity of alveolospheres.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that Nox4-/+ aged L-MSCs have improved ATP/ADP ratios (Figure 4D) and restored TCA cycle metabolites (Figure 4E-F) compared to wild-type aged L-MSCs.

claim: Nox4 downregulation restored the self-organizing capacity of alveolospheres.
source: The reactive oxygen species generating enzyme, NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4), was highly activated in aged L-MSCs and Nox4 downregulation was sufficient to, at least partially, reverse this age-related energy deficit, while restoring the self-organizing capacity of alveolospheres.
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data showing that young AEC2s co-cultured with aged Nox4-/+ L-MSCs form larger and more numerous alveolospheres compared to those with wild-type aged L-MSCs (Figure 4I-K).

claim: Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC2s) serve as facultative stem/progenitor cells in adult mammalian lungs.
source: Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC2s) serve as facultative stem/progenitor cells in adult mammalian lungs and differentiate into type 1 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC1s) in response to diverse injuries to reconstitute and reestablish the alveolar gas exchange surface (Barkauskas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barkauskas et al., 2013, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: AEC2s differentiate into type 1 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC1s) in response to diverse injuries to reconstitute and reestablish the alveolar gas exchange surface.
source: Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC2s) serve as facultative stem/progenitor cells in adult mammalian lungs and differentiate into type 1 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC1s) in response to diverse injuries to reconstitute and reestablish the alveolar gas exchange surface (Barkauskas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barkauskas et al., 2013, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: AEC2 regenerative capacity declines with age.
source: AEC2 regenerative capacity declines with age, resulting in impaired lung injury repair responses, thus increasing susceptibility to various lung diseases (Schulte et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schulte et al., 2019 and Watson et al., 2020, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Age-related decline in AEC2 regenerative capacity results in impaired lung injury repair responses.
source: AEC2 regenerative capacity declines with age, resulting in impaired lung injury repair responses, thus increasing susceptibility to various lung diseases (Schulte et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schulte et al., 2019 and Watson et al., 2020, and represents a logical inference from the decline in regenerative capacity.

claim: Impaired lung injury repair responses increase susceptibility to various lung diseases.
source: AEC2 regenerative capacity declines with age, resulting in impaired lung injury repair responses, thus increasing susceptibility to various lung diseases (Schulte et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schulte et al., 2019 and Watson et al., 2020, and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Alveolospheres with a single layer of epithelial cells composed of both AEC2s (SFTPC-positive) and AEC1s (T1α-positive) surrounding a hollow sphere typically form 9–12 days following co-culture.
source: alveolospheres with a single layer of epithelial cells composed of both AEC2s (surfactant protein C [SFTPC]-positive) and AEC1s (lung type I integral membrane glycoprotein [T1α]-positive) surrounding a hollow sphere typically form 9–12 days following co-culture (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alveolosphere assay and immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: L-MSCs expressing PDGFRα were found primarily in cells lining the outer edges of alveolospheres.
source: L-MSCs expressing platelet-derived growth factor receptor-α (PDFGRα), with a fewer number expressing α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), were found primarily in cells lining the outer edges of alveolospheres (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A fewer number of L-MSCs express α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) in alveolospheres.
source: L-MSCs expressing platelet-derived growth factor receptor-α (PDFGRα), with a fewer number expressing α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), were found primarily in cells lining the outer edges of alveolospheres (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AEC2s within alveolospheres stain for the cell proliferation marker, Ki-67.
source: AEC2s within alveolospheres stained for both the cell proliferation marker, Ki-67, and the double-strand DNA damage repair marker, histone H2A.X, suggesting ongoing AEC2 turnover within these 3D organoids (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: AEC2s within alveolospheres stain for the double-strand DNA damage repair marker, histone H2A.X.
source: AEC2s within alveolospheres stained for both the cell proliferation marker, Ki-67, and the double-strand DNA damage repair marker, histone H2A.X, suggesting ongoing AEC2 turnover within these 3D organoids (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ki-67 and histone H2A.X staining suggest ongoing AEC2 turnover within alveolospheres.
source: AEC2s within alveolospheres stained for both the cell proliferation marker, Ki-67, and the double-strand DNA damage repair marker, histone H2A.X, suggesting ongoing AEC2 turnover within these 3D organoids (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the presence of proliferation and DNA repair markers shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: The self-organizing behavior of L-MSCs and AEC2s is critically dependent on the presence of both cell types.
source: This self-organizing behavior of L-MSCs and AEC2s is critically dependent on the presence of both cell types as AEC2s in the absence of AEC2s do not self-organize to form alveolospheres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrating that AEC2s alone do not form alveolospheres.

claim: AEC2s in the absence of L-MSCs do not self-organize to form alveolospheres.
source: This self-organizing behavior of L-MSCs and AEC2s is critically dependent on the presence of both cell types as AEC2s in the absence of AEC2s do not self-organize to form alveolospheres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: L-MSCs and AEC2s from young mice generated normal alveolospheres.
source: L-MSCs and AEC2s from young mice generated normal alveolospheres, whereas L-MSCs and AEC2s from the lungs of aged mice showed impaired self-organization with condensed, poorly formed organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alveolosphere assay shown in Figure 1H.

claim: L-MSCs and AEC2s from the lungs of aged mice showed impaired self-organization with condensed, poorly formed organoids.
source: L-MSCs and AEC2s from young mice generated normal alveolospheres, whereas L-MSCs and AEC2s from the lungs of aged mice showed impaired self-organization with condensed, poorly formed organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alveolosphere assay shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Combining aged AEC2s with young L-MSCs resulted in relatively normal-appearing alveolospheres.
source: Interestingly, combining aged AEC2s with young L-MSCs resulted in relatively normal-appearing alveolospheres, while the reverse combination (young AEC2s and old L-MSCs) did not (Figure 1H, middle and lower panels; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alveolosphere assay shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The combination of young AEC2s and old L-MSCs did not result in normal-appearing alveolospheres.
source: Interestingly, combining aged AEC2s with young L-MSCs resulted in relatively normal-appearing alveolospheres, while the reverse combination (young AEC2s and old L-MSCs) did not (Figure 1H, middle and lower panels; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alveolosphere assay shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of alveolospheres formed was not significantly different between groups with different combinations of young and aged L-MSCs and AEC2s.
source: Quantitative analyses revealed that, while the number of alveolospheres formed was not significantly different between groups (Figure 1I), the size of alveolospheres was critically dependent on the age of L-MSCs, and not that of AEC2s (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The size of alveolospheres was critically dependent on the age of L-MSCs, and not that of AEC2s.
source: Quantitative analyses revealed that, while the number of alveolospheres formed was not significantly different between groups (Figure 1I), the size of alveolospheres was critically dependent on the age of L-MSCs, and not that of AEC2s (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1J demonstrating that alveolosphere size depends on L-MSC age.

claim: Secreted factor(s) from young L-MSCs are capable of supporting the self-organizing behavior of alveolospheres.
source: These findings indicate that secreted factor(s) from young L-MSCs are capable of supporting the self-organizing behavior of alveolospheres, while aged L-MSCs do not.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that young L-MSCs support alveolosphere formation with both young and aged AEC2s (Figure 1H-J).

claim: Aged L-MSCs do not support the self-organizing behavior of alveolospheres.
source: These findings indicate that secreted factor(s) from young L-MSCs are capable of supporting the self-organizing behavior of alveolospheres, while aged L-MSCs do not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that aged L-MSCs fail to support normal alveolosphere formation (Figure 1H-J).

claim: Cellular senescence accumulates in tissues with advancing age.
source: Cellular senescence accumulates in tissues with advancing age (Krishnamurthy et al., 2004) and has been proposed as a key driver of aging and aging-related disease phenotypes (Baker et al., 2016; Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krishnamurthy et al., 2004, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cellular senescence has been proposed as a key driver of aging and aging-related disease phenotypes.

claim: Aged L-MSCs show senescent features in monolayer 2D cell culture as confirmed by β-galactosidase staining.
source: First, we confirmed the senescent features of L-MSCs from aged mice in monolayer 2D cell culture (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in 3D alveolospheres (Figure 2B) by staining for β-galactosidase (β-gal) (Dimri et al., 1995) and lipofuscin (Georgakopoulou et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with citation to Dimri et al., 1995 for the method.

claim: Aged L-MSCs show senescent features in 3D alveolospheres as confirmed by lipofuscin staining.

evidence: This claim is supported by lipofuscin staining data shown in Figure 2B, with citation to Georgakopoulou et al., 2013 for the method.

claim: IL-6 is released at higher levels by aged L-MSCs compared to young L-MSCs.

evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine array data shown in Figure 2D and E.

evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine array data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: 503 high-confidence proteins were identified by mass spectrometry-based discovery proteomics of L-MSC secretome.
source: After adjustments for false discovery rates, 503 high-confidence proteins were identified; of these, 235 proteins were found to have non-zero quantifiable values in at least three of four experimental repeats per group for subsequent statistical analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data described in the text and shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: 235 proteins were found to have non-zero quantifiable values in at least three of four experimental repeats per group in the L-MSC secretome analysis.
source: After adjustments for false discovery rates, 503 high-confidence proteins were identified; of these, 235 proteins were found to have non-zero quantifiable values in at least three of four experimental repeats per group for subsequent statistical analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data described in the text.

claim: 36 proteins passed both a single pairwise statistical test (p<0.05) and a fold change of ±1.5 in the comparison between young and aged L-MSC secretomes.
source: The 36 proteins that passed both a single pairwise statistical test (p<0.05) in addition to a fold change of ±1.5 (Supplementary file 1A) were subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) (Figure 2G) and heat map analysis (Figure 2H; quantitation of heat map proteins, Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 2G-I and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Gene ontology localization analyses of L-MSC secretome revealed enrichment in secreted proteins, including extracellular vesicles and extracellular matrix.
source: Gene ontology localization analyses revealed enrichment in secreted proteins, including extracellular vesicles and extracellular matrix (Supplementary file 1B); interestingly, gene ontology processes analysis indicated the top cellular processes as negative regulation of reactive oxygen species metabolic process and extracellular matrix/structure organization (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data as described in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Gene ontology processes analysis indicated the top cellular processes as negative regulation of reactive oxygen species metabolic process and extracellular matrix/structure organization.

evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data as described in Supplementary file 1C.

claim: Enrichment by top toxic pathologies revealed proteins associated with lung fibrosis in aged L-MSC secretome.
source: Enrichment by top toxic pathologies revealed proteins associated with lung fibrosis (Supplementary file 1D), a disease associated with aging (Thannickal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data as described in Supplementary file 1D.

claim: Lung fibrosis is a disease associated with aging.
source: Enrichment by top toxic pathologies revealed proteins associated with lung fibrosis (Supplementary file 1D), a disease associated with aging (Thannickal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thannickal et al., 2014, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Network analysis revealed upregulation of pathways associated with the canonical WNT-signaling pathway and cell cycle regulation in aged L-MSC secretome.

claim: Aged L-MSCs are characterized by cellular senescence associated with SASP factors, oxidative stress, and alterations in regenerative pathways that may account for impaired alveolosphere formation.
source: Together, these findings suggest that aged L-MSCs are characterized by cellular senescence associated with SASP factors, oxidative stress, and alterations in regenerative pathways that may account for impaired alveolosphere formation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data from senescence markers, cytokine arrays, and proteomics analyses (Figures 2A-I).

claim: Altered cellular metabolism has been linked to both senescence and aging.
source: Altered cellular metabolism has been linked to both senescence and aging (López-Otín et al., 2016; Finkel, 2015; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to López-Otín et al., 2016, Finkel, 2015, and Sun et al., 2016, representing established knowledge in the field.

evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Real-time extracellular acidification rates (ECAR) were significantly higher in aged L-MSCs as compared to young L-MSCs.
source: Real-time oxygen consumption rates (OCR) and extracellular acidification rates (ECAR) were significantly higher in aged L-MSCs as compared to young L-MSCs (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Aged L-MSCs showed significantly higher basal respiration when compared to young L-MSCs.
source: Aged L-MSCs showed significantly higher basal, maximal, ATP-linked, proton leak, and non-mitochondrial respiration when compared to young L-MSCs with no change in reserve capacity (Figure 3C-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Aged L-MSCs showed significantly higher maximal respiration when compared to young L-MSCs.
source: Aged L-MSCs showed significantly higher basal, maximal, ATP-linked, proton leak, and non-mitochondrial respiration when compared to young L-MSCs with no change in reserve capacity (Figure 3C-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Aged L-MSCs showed significantly higher ATP-linked respiration when compared to young L-MSCs.

claim: Aged L-MSCs showed significantly higher proton leak when compared to young L-MSCs.

claim: Aged L-MSCs showed no change in reserve capacity when compared to young L-MSCs.

evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Higher non-mitochondrial OCRs in aged L-MSCs suggest potential activation of oxygen-metabolizing NADPH oxidases in aged L-MSCs.
source: Higher non-mitochondrial OCRs in aged L-MSCs suggest potential activation of oxygen-metabolizing NADPH oxidases in aged L-MSCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of higher non-mitochondrial OCR in aged L-MSCs (Figure 3H).

claim: An energy map profile of the OCR and ECAR data indicated a higher basal rate of both mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis in aged L-MSCs.
source: An energy map profile of the OCR and ECAR data indicated a higher basal rate of both mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis (Figure 3I), suggesting that aged L-MSCs are under a basal state of higher metabolic demand.
evidence: This claim is supported by the energy map shown in Figure 3I derived from OCR and ECAR data.

claim: Aged L-MSCs are under a basal state of higher metabolic demand.
source: An energy map profile of the OCR and ECAR data indicated a higher basal rate of both mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis (Figure 3I), suggesting that aged L-MSCs are under a basal state of higher metabolic demand.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the energy map data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Higher energy demand under conditions of equivalent nutrient supply was associated with reduced levels of ATP/ADP under steady-state basal conditions in aged L-MSCs.
source: This higher energy demand under conditions of equivalent nutrient supply was associated with reduced levels of ATP/ADP under steady-state basal conditions (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP/ADP ratio measurements shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Despite similar basal ECAR, higher rates of maximal and non-glycolysis related ECAR were observed in aged L-MSCs.
source: Measurement of ECAR indicated that, despite similar basal ECAR, higher rates of maximal and non-glycolysis related ECAR were observed in aged L-MSCs. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ECAR measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Senescence of L-MSCs is characterized by higher baseline metabolic demand with reduced bioenergetic efficiency.
source: Together, these data indicate that senescence of L-MSCs is characterized by higher baseline metabolic demand with reduced bioenergetic efficiency.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined metabolic data from Figures 3A-J showing higher OCR/ECAR but lower ATP/ADP ratios.

claim: Replication-induced senescence of human lung fibroblasts results in higher rates of extracellular H2O2 release in association with increased expression of NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4).
source: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) has emerged as critical regulator of redox signaling and oxidative stress (Sies, 2017). Replication-induced senescence of human lung fibroblasts results in higher rates of extracellular H2O2 release in association with increased expression of NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4) (Sanders et al., 2015), a gene that is inducible by the pro-senescent/pro-fibrotic mediator, transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) (Hecker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanders et al., 2015, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nox4 is a gene that is inducible by the pro-senescent/pro-fibrotic mediator, transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1).
source: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) has emerged as critical regulator of redox signaling and oxidative stress (Sies, 2017). Replication-induced senescence of human lung fibroblasts results in higher rates of extracellular H2O2 release in association with increased expression of NADPH oxidase 4 (Nox4) (Sanders et al., 2015), a gene that is inducible by the pro-senescent/pro-fibrotic mediator, transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) (Hecker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hecker et al., 2009, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Aged (22–24 months old) L-MSCs released higher baseline levels of H2O2 compared to young (3 months old) L-MSCs.
source: We explored whether L-MSCs isolated from naturally aged mice are associated with higher Nox4-dependent H2O2 secretion; in comparison to young (3 months old) L-MSCs, aged (22–24 months old), L-MSCs released higher baseline levels of H2O2, an effect that was further stimulated by exogenous stimulation with TGF-β1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by H2O2 release assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H2O2 release from aged L-MSCs was further stimulated by exogenous stimulation with TGF-β1.
source: We explored whether L-MSCs isolated from naturally aged mice are associated with higher Nox4-dependent H2O2 secretion; in comparison to young (3 months old) L-MSCs, aged (22–24 months old), L-MSCs released higher baseline levels of H2O2, an effect that was further stimulated by exogenous stimulation with TGF-β1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by H2O2 release assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The age-dependent, pro-oxidant phenotype of L-MSCs was markedly reduced in aged mice heterozygous for Nox4 (Nox4-/+).
source: This age-dependent, pro-oxidant phenotype of L-MSCs was markedly reduced in aged mice heterozygous for Nox4 (Nox4-/+; Figure 4B and C), implicating Nox4 as a critical mediator of both basal and TGF-β1-induced H2O2 release.
evidence: This claim is supported by H2O2 release assay data shown in Figure 4B and C comparing aged wild-type and Nox4-/+ L-MSCs.

claim: Nox4 is a critical mediator of both basal and TGF-β1-induced H2O2 release in aged L-MSCs.
source: This age-dependent, pro-oxidant phenotype of L-MSCs was markedly reduced in aged mice heterozygous for Nox4 (Nox4-/+; Figure 4B and C), implicating Nox4 as a critical mediator of both basal and TGF-β1-induced H2O2 release.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Nox4 haploinsufficiency reduces H2O2 release (Figure 4B and C).

claim: A bolus addition of H2O2 (1 µM) to organoid culture comprising young AEC2s and young L-MSCs resulted in a decrease in the size of alveolospheres.
source: Although it is difficult to replicate the tonic, continuous release of H2O2 from a constitutive enzymatic source such as Nox4 in metabolically active cells, we tested the effect of a bolus addition of H2O2 (1 µM) to organoid culture comprising young AEC2s and young L-MSCs; this resulted in a decrease in the size of alveolospheres, without significantly affecting the numbers of alveolospheres formed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: A bolus addition of H2O2 (1 µM) to organoid culture comprising young AEC2s and young L-MSCs did not significantly affect the numbers of alveolospheres formed.
source: Although it is difficult to replicate the tonic, continuous release of H2O2 from a constitutive enzymatic source such as Nox4 in metabolically active cells, we tested the effect of a bolus addition of H2O2 (1 µM) to organoid culture comprising young AEC2s and young L-MSCs; this resulted in a decrease in the size of alveolospheres, without significantly affecting the numbers of alveolospheres formed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Recent studies implicate Nox4 in metabolic reprogramming.

claim: The reduced levels of ATP/ADP in aged L-MSCs were partially rescued in age-matched Nox4-/+ L-MSCs.

claim: Nox4 plays a role in the reduced bioenergetic efficiency associated with aging in L-MSCs.
source: The reduced levels of ATP/ADP in aged L-MSCs were partially rescued in age-matched Nox4-/+ L-MSCs (Figure 4D), implicating a role for Nox4 in the reduced bioenergetic efficiency associated with aging.

claim: The steady-state levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite malate were reduced in wild-type aged L-MSCs.
source: The steady-state levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolites, malate and citrate, were reduced in wild-type aged L-MSCs; these levels recovered to levels similar to young L-MSCs in Nox4-/+ L-MSCs, although only malate achieved statistical significance (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The steady-state levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite citrate were reduced in wild-type aged L-MSCs.
source: The steady-state levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolites, malate and citrate, were reduced in wild-type aged L-MSCs; these levels recovered to levels similar to young L-MSCs in Nox4-/+ L-MSCs, although only malate achieved statistical significance (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Malate and citrate levels recovered to levels similar to young L-MSCs in Nox4-/+ L-MSCs, although only malate achieved statistical significance.

evidence: This claim is supported by targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Levels of other TCA metabolites that were not significantly altered with aging in L-MSCs were not affected by a deficiency in Nox4.

evidence: This claim is supported by targeted metabolomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-G.

claim: β-gal activity was found to be significantly lower in Nox4-deficient aged L-MSCs as compared to wild-type aged L-MSCs.
source: β-gal activity was found to be significantly lower in Nox4-deficient aged L-MSCs as compared to wild-type aged L-MSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Protein (antibody-based) arrays showed significant downregulation of SASP-associated cytokines in aged Nox4-/+ L-MSCs vs. aged L-MSCs.
source: In addition to metabolic dysfunction, an important feature of senescence reprogramming is the activation of a SASP program. We determined whether Nox4 modulates the release of cytokines/growth factors by aged L-MSCs. Protein (antibody-based) arrays showed significant downregulation of SASP-associated cytokines in aged Nox4-/+ L-MSCs vs. aged L-MSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine array data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Nox4 haploinsufficiency in aged L-MSCs resulted in significant downregulation of OCR as compared to aged L-MSCs.
source: Interestingly, Nox4 haploinsufficiency in aged L-MSCs resulted in significant downregulation of OCR as compared to aged L-MSCs (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Nox4-/+ aged L-MSCs showed significantly lower basal respiration compared to wild-type aged L-MSCs.

evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF Analyzer data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Nox4 contributes to metabolic dysfunction, bioenergetic inefficiency, and SASP programming in L-MSC aging.
source: Together, these studies indicate that Nox4 contributes to metabolic dysfunction, bioenergetic inefficiency, and SASP programming in L-MSC aging.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing that Nox4 deficiency improves ATP/ADP ratios, TCA metabolites, OCR, and reduces SASP factors (Figure 4D-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).

claim: The aberrant formation of alveolospheres when young AEC2s were cultured with aged L-MSCs were rescued when replaced with age-matched Nox4-/+ L-MSCs.
source: Based on the observations that Nox4 alters cellular bioenergetics of L-MSCs, we examined the effects of Nox4 on regulating the self-organizing potential of alveolospheres. The aberrant formation of alveolospheres when young AEC2s were cultured with aged L-MSCs were rescued when replaced with age-matched Nox4-/+ L-MSCs (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J); quantitation of both alveolospheres counts (Figure 4J) and alveolosphere size (Figure 4K) was significantly enhanced when these assays were conducted with Nox4-deficient L-MSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Quantitation of both alveolospheres counts was significantly enhanced when assays were conducted with Nox4-deficient L-MSCs.
source: Based on the observations that Nox4 alters cellular bioenergetics of L-MSCs, we examined the effects of Nox4 on regulating the self-organizing potential of alveolospheres. The aberrant formation of alveolospheres when young AEC2s were cultured with aged L-MSCs were rescued when replaced with age-matched Nox4-/+ L-MSCs (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J); quantitation of both alveolospheres counts (Figure 4J) and alveolosphere size (Figure 4K) was significantly enhanced when these assays were conducted with Nox4-deficient L-MSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Quantitation of alveolosphere size was significantly enhanced when assays were conducted with Nox4-deficient L-MSCs.
source: Based on the observations that Nox4 alters cellular bioenergetics of L-MSCs, we examined the effects of Nox4 on regulating the self-organizing potential of alveolospheres. The aberrant formation of alveolospheres when young AEC2s were cultured with aged L-MSCs were rescued when replaced with age-matched Nox4-/+ L-MSCs (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J); quantitation of both alveolospheres counts (Figure 4J) and alveolosphere size (Figure 4K) was significantly enhanced when these assays were conducted with Nox4-deficient L-MSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The Nox4 inhibitor GKT137831 (10 µM) did not result in significant changes in alveolosphere formation when added to an organoid culture system of young AEC2s and aged L-MSCs.
source: We were also unable to detect significant changes in alveolosphere formation when the Nox4 inhibitor, GKT137831 (10 µM), was added to an organoid culture system of young AEC2s and aged L-MSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-M); however, it is difficult to ascertain whether this intervention effectively inhibited Nox4 activity in this organoid model.
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-M.

claim: The phenotype of impaired alveolosphere formation in young AECs and aged L-MSCs was reversed by haploinsufficiency of Nox4 in L-MSCs.
source: While the phenotype of impaired alveolosphere formation in young AECs and aged L-MSCs was reversed by haploinsufficiency of Nox4 in L-MSCs (Figure 4I–K), this was not sufficient to completely reverse the phenotype in aged AEC2s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N-P).
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 4I–K.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Nox4 in L-MSCs was not sufficient to completely reverse the phenotype of impaired alveolosphere formation in aged AEC2s.
source: While the phenotype of impaired alveolosphere formation in young AECs and aged L-MSCs was reversed by haploinsufficiency of Nox4 in L-MSCs (Figure 4I–K), this was not sufficient to completely reverse the phenotype in aged AEC2s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N-P).
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1N-P.

claim: Wild-type young L-MSCs are sufficient to reverse the aged AEC2 phenotype.
source: This finding, along with the observation that wild-type young L-MSCs are sufficient to reverse the aged AEC2 phenotype (Figure 1H), suggests that in addition to reduced expression of Nox4 in aged L-MSCs, the young mesenchyme may support niche function and recovery of alveolosphere formation of aged AEC2s through Nox4-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by alveolosphere assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The young mesenchyme may support niche function and recovery of alveolosphere formation of aged AEC2s through Nox4-independent mechanisms.
source: This finding, along with the observation that wild-type young L-MSCs are sufficient to reverse the aged AEC2 phenotype (Figure 1H), suggests that in addition to reduced expression of Nox4 in aged L-MSCs, the young mesenchyme may support niche function and recovery of alveolosphere formation of aged AEC2s through Nox4-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that young L-MSCs rescue aged AEC2 phenotype (Figure 1H) but Nox4 deficiency alone does not fully rescue aged AEC2 phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N-P).

claim: An aging alveolar stem cell niche may involve both a gain of 'pro-senescent factors' (Nox4) and loss of 'rejuvenation factors' by the mesenchyme.
source: Thus, an aging alveolar stem cell niche may involve both a gain of 'pro-senescent factors' (Nox4) and loss of 'rejuvenation factors' by the mesenchyme; the identification of the latter will require further study.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined observations that Nox4 deficiency partially rescues the phenotype and young L-MSCs fully rescue the phenotype.

claim: Nox4-dependent oxidative stress, senescence, and bioenergetic insufficiency play a critical role in restricting the capacity for cellular self-organization in a 3D organoid model of aging and stem/progenitor cell function.
source: Together, our studies support a critical role for Nox4-dependent oxidative stress, senescence, and bioenergetic insufficiency in restricting the capacity for cellular self-organization in a 3D organoid model of aging and stem/progenitor cell function (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data from all experiments showing that Nox4 affects oxidative stress, senescence, bioenergetics, and alveolosphere formation.

claim: A fundamental difference between non-living matter and life forms on our planet is the ability to extract energy from the environment, primarily through oxidation of carbon-based fuels.
source: A fundamental difference between non-living matter and life forms on our planet is the ability to extract energy from the environment, primarily through oxidation of carbon-based fuels.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in biology and thermodynamics.

claim: The second law of thermodynamics that governs both living and non-living matter does not strictly apply to living organisms capable of self-renewal through the continuous and dynamic exchange of energy and mass.
source: Thus, the second law of thermodynamics that governs both living and non-living matter does not strictly apply to living organisms capable of self-renewal through the continuous and dynamic exchange of energy (from exogenous nutrients) and mass (biosynthetic and degradative processes in respiring tissues/organs).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in thermodynamics and biology.

claim: When the capacity for energy-dependent self-renewal is diminished, the law of entropic degeneration will be operative in living organisms.
source: It follows then that, when this capacity for energy-dependent self-renewal is diminished, the law of entropic degeneration will be operative in living organisms.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on thermodynamic principles applied to biological systems.

claim: Aging is associated with derangements in metabolism that influences, and may in fact control, many of the well-recognized hallmarks of aging, including cellular senescence.
source: Aging is associated with derangements in metabolism that influences, and may in fact control, many of the well-recognized hallmarks of aging, including cellular senescence (López-Otín et al., 2016; López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to López-Otín et al., 2016 and López-Otín et al., 2013, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The inter-relatedness of metabolism with traditional aging hallmarks is difficult to untangle due to complexities of studies in living organisms and the relative simplicity of 2D cell culture models.
source: The inter-relatedness of metabolism with these traditional aging hallmarks is difficult to untangle due to complexities of studies in living organisms and the relative simplicity of 2D cell culture models.
evidence: This claim represents a methodological challenge in the field as stated by the authors.

claim: Organoids offer the opportunity to study complex living phenomena such as emergent properties and self-organization in biological systems while allowing for reductionist approaches that provide mechanistic understanding.
source: Organoids offer the opportunity to study complex living phenomena such as emergent properties and self-organization in biological systems while at the same time allowing for reductionist approaches that provide mechanistic understanding of these complex processes.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the utility of organoid models in biological research.

claim: Nox4 plays a critical role in regulating cellular bioenergetics and senescence that limits stem cell function.
source: Using a combination of methods that included a 3D organoid model, biochemical approaches, proteomics, and gene targeting, we demonstrate a critical role for the oxygen metabolizing enzyme, Nox4, in regulating cellular bioenergetics and senescence that limits stem cell function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from the study showing that Nox4 affects bioenergetics, senescence, and alveolosphere formation.

claim: Nox4 may function as an antagonistically pleiotropic gene and contribute to a number of age-related degenerative disorders, including fibrotic diseases.
source: Consistent with contemporary theories on aging, Nox4 may function as an antagonistically pleiotropic gene and contribute a number of age-related degenerative disorders, including fibrotic diseases (Thannickal, 2010; Lambeth, 2007).
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the current findings and citations to Thannickal, 2010 and Lambeth, 2007.

claim: Proteomic analyses of proteins secreted by aged L-MSCs suggested alterations in cellular redox/oxidative stress from gene ontology analysis.
source: Interestingly, proteomic analyses of proteins secreted by aged L-MSCs in the current study suggested alterations in cellular redox/oxidative stress (from gene ontology analysis) and lung fibrosis (as a 'toxic pathology').
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data as described in the text.

claim: Proteomic analyses of proteins secreted by aged L-MSCs suggested lung fibrosis as a 'toxic pathology'.

evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data as described in the text.

claim: Intercellular communication and stem cell exhaustion are important hallmarks of aging.
source: These findings, as well as candidate SASP factors, highlight the emerging importance of intercellular communication and stem cell exhaustion as important hallmarks of aging (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to López-Otín et al., 2013, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Regenerative mechanisms in adult, mammalian organisms primarily rely on the activation and differentiation of tissue/organ-resident stem cells.
source: Regenerative mechanisms in adult, mammalian organisms primarily rely on the activation and differentiation of tissue/organ-resident stem cells (Hogan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hogan et al., 2014, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Homeostatic maintenance of stem cells requires a tightly regulated niche that includes other supporting cell types, in particular stromal cells.
source: Homeostatic maintenance of these stem cells requires a tightly regulated niche that includes other supporting cell types, in particular stromal cells (Basil et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Basil et al., 2020, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: L-MSC aging, relative to AEC aging, largely accounts for the age-related inability to form alveolospheres.
source: An important finding from our studies is the observation that L-MSC aging, relative to AEC aging, largely accounts for the age-related inability to form alveolospheres.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that the age of L-MSCs, not AEC2s, determines alveolosphere size (Figure 1H-J).

claim: Aging of the stem cell niche may be as important, and perhaps more decisive, in promoting certain age-related pathologies.
source: Thus, aging of the stem cell niche may be as important, and perhaps more decisive, in promoting certain age-related pathologies.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that L-MSC aging is more critical than AEC2 aging for alveolosphere formation.

claim: Therapeutic targeting of metabolic aging within the stem cell niche, specifically that of lung-resident fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, may offer a more effective and viable strategy for age-related degenerative disorders such as tissue/organ fibrosis.
source: Therapeutic targeting of metabolic aging within the stem cell niche, specifically that of lung-resident fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, may offer a more effective and viable strategy for age-related degenerative disorders such as tissue/organ fibrosis.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the findings that L-MSC aging and Nox4-dependent metabolic dysfunction impair alveolosphere formation.

claim: Self-organization in biological systems is a process by which cells reduce their internal entropy and maintain order within dynamic, self-renewing systems.
source: Self-organization in biological systems is a process by which cells reduce their internal entropy and maintain order within these dynamic, self-renewing systems (Chatterjee et al., 2017; Kiss et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chatterjee et al., 2017 and Kiss et al., 2009, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Exhaustion of stem/progenitor cells, cellular senescence, and altered intercellular communication have been proposed as aging hallmarks that increase susceptibility to age-related disorders.
source: Exhaustion of stem/progenitor cells, cellular senescence, and altered intercellular communication have been proposed as aging hallmarks that increase susceptibility to age-related disorders (Schultz and Sinclair, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schultz and Sinclair, 2016, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The interactions between aging hallmarks and whether cellular bioenergetics associated with cellular senescence may account for age-associated stem cell dysfunction and altered cell-cell communication have not been well defined.
source: However, the interactions between these hallmarks and whether cellular bioenergetics associated with cellular senescence may account for age-associated stem cell dysfunction and altered cell-cell communication have not been well defined.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap in the field as stated by the authors.

claim: Cellular bioenergetics and redox imbalance are critical drivers of inter-dependent aging hallmarks.
source: In this study, we utilized an organoid model to study stem cell behavior and intercellular communication that may account for age-related phenotypes; through these studies, we identify cellular bioenergetics and redox imbalance as critical drivers of these inter-dependent aging hallmarks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from the study showing that Nox4-dependent redox imbalance affects bioenergetics, senescence, and alveolosphere formation.

claim: The mammalian lung serves an essential role in organismal metabolism by serving as the primary organ for systemic exchange of oxygen for carbon dioxide.
source: The mammalian lung serves an essential role in organismal metabolism, uniquely by serving as the primary organ for systemic exchange of oxygen for carbon dioxide.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in physiology.

claim: Regeneration and maintenance of structure-function of the lung are dependent on adult, tissue-resident stem cells that reside in unique niches along the airways.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Basil et al., 2020 and Hogan et al., 2014, representing established knowledge in the field.
